hero.name: Kavya
hero.who: a Class 12 student in Kota who thinks exercise steals precious study time

story.b: Kavya moved to Kota from Bhopal last year for medical entrance coaching. She lives in a hostel room with a tiny window, and her days are classes, tests and fourteen hours at a desk. She stopped playing badminton the week she arrived, because every hour outside felt like an hour lost. Now her back aches, her mind feels foggy by afternoon, and she rereads the same biology page three times. Before the weekly tests her heart races and she sleeps badly. Her mother suggests a walk. Kavya almost laughs. Her rank is slipping, and walking feels like the last thing a serious student should do. Exercise, to her, is for losing weight, not for cracking exams.

ask.q: Kavya feels foggy and stressed but believes exercise wastes study time. What should she reconsider?
o: That movement is only about weight, when it may also help her brain and mood
That she needs even more hours at the desk to beat the fog
That stress before tests is normal and nothing can be done about it
ask.why: More desk hours on a foggy brain often mean rereading the same page, and accepting the stress leaves her stuck. Movement does more than burn calories. For many people it seems to help focus, mood and pressure, so a little of it may make her study hours count for more.

chapters.take: Exercise is not only for your body. It may help your brain too.

story.b: Kavya decides to test her mother's idea, but on her own terms. Before her evening chemistry session, she spends ten minutes skipping on the hostel terrace with a rope borrowed from her roommate Ruchi. She feels silly, sweaty and out of breath. Then she sits down with organic chemistry, the chapter she dreads. She notices she reads the reaction steps with a little more energy, and two of them stick on the first try. One evening proves nothing, so she keeps a note for two weeks of days with skipping and days without. Her notes suggest the skipping days are usually the better study evenings. Those ten minutes, she realises, may be warming up her mind.

ask.q: Ruchi has a tough physics chapter tonight and plans to start straight after dinner. What small change might help?
o: Drink two strong coffees so she can push through late
Do ten minutes of brisk movement, then begin the chapter
Skip dinner and use the extra time for more study
ask.why: Extra coffee may leave her jittery and sleepless, and skipping dinner usually drains energy instead of saving time. A short burst of brisk movement before studying can leave the mind more alert and ready to take things in, so the hours that follow may count for more.

chapters.take: A short burst of movement before study can help your mind get ready.

story.b: The weekly test goes badly. Kavya scores lower than last time, and her chest feels tight all evening. Normally she would lie on her bed scrolling through toppers' videos, which only makes it worse. This time she laces her shoes and walks fast around the hostel lane, past the poha stall and the photocopy shop, for fifteen minutes. The tightness eases a little. She starts taking a brisk walk most evenings, not only on bad days. Over the next weeks she notices that test days still make her nervous, but the nerves feel smaller, and she bounces back faster afterwards. The pressure has not changed. She just seems to carry it differently, as if her body has had some practice.

ask.q: After a stressful mock test, Ruchi plans to stay in bed scrolling all evening. What might help her more?
o: Scroll toppers' videos to feel motivated for the next test
Study late into the night to make up for the low score
Take a brisk walk, and make regular movement part of her week
ask.why: Scrolling toppers can deepen comparison and worry, and late-night study on a stressed mind often goes poorly. A brisk walk can help her body settle after stress, and regular exercise may help her handle future pressure better, so tests hit a little less hard.

chapters.take: Regular movement may help your body carry stress more lightly.

story.b: Kavya notices that Ruchi has been quiet for weeks. She skips meals, stays in bed on Sundays and once says nothing seems to matter anymore. Kavya is worried. She remembers how much better she feels after moving, so she invites Ruchi for badminton at the colony court on Sunday morning. Ruchi comes slowly, and even laughs once when the shuttle lands in a tree. Kavya also knows a game is not enough for something like this. Afterwards, sitting on the steps with two glasses of lassi, she gently tells Ruchi that the coaching centre has a counsellor, and offers to go with her. Ruchi agrees. Badminton becomes a weekly thing, alongside the counselling, not instead of it.

ask.q: Ruchi has felt low for weeks. What is the most caring thing Kavya can do?
o: Tell her exercise will fix it, so she does not need anyone else
Invite her to move together, and gently encourage her to see a counsellor or doctor
Leave her alone, since low moods always pass on their own
ask.why: Exercise can lift mood for many people, but it is not a replacement for proper help when someone has felt low for weeks. Leaving her alone can make her feel more isolated. Moving together offers comfort and a lift, while a counsellor or doctor can give the support she may need.

chapters.take: Movement can lift mood, but it works best alongside proper support, not instead of it.

story.b: Every day around three, in the long afternoon lecture, Kavya's attention slides. The teacher's voice blurs, and she copies notes without understanding them. She used to fix this with a second cup of sweet canteen tea. Now she tries something else. In the ten-minute break she climbs the coaching building's stairs, four floors up and down, twice. When she sits again, her mind feels clearer and she follows the next derivation more easily. On a call home to Bhopal, she learns her younger brother Yash has the same trouble with homework. Their mother has started sending him to play football in the colony for half an hour first. He sits down calmer, she says, and finishes faster.

ask.q: Kavya's friend keeps losing focus during long evening revision. What should she try first?
o: Keep forcing herself to sit still until the chapter is done
Drink an energy drink every evening to stay sharp
Get up and move for five minutes when her focus starts slipping
ask.why: Forcing herself through the slump often means reading without absorbing, and daily energy drinks may disturb sleep. Short bursts of movement can refresh attention for many people, so a few minutes of stairs or stretching may bring focus back better than pushing on. If tiredness lasts, a doctor can help.

chapters.take: When focus slips, a few minutes of movement may help more than another cup of tea.

story.b: During the Diwali holidays, Kavya goes home to Bhopal. Her nani, seventy-one, says she has become forgetful and mostly sits watching TV. Kavya has read that exercise may help keep the brain healthier with age, especially activities that involve learning new moves. She finds a gentle morning yoga group in the park near their house, mostly retired women. Because Nani has knee pain, they first ask her doctor, who says gentle yoga is fine with care. On the first morning Nani mixes up left and right and laughs at herself. By the end of the holidays she has learned four new poses and a short breathing routine, and she calls Kavya in Kota to describe each one.

ask.q: Kavya's grandfather wants to stay sharp in his seventies but has a heart condition. What is the best plan?
o: Check with his doctor, then try a gentle activity that teaches new moves
Start an intense daily workout to build strength quickly
Avoid all movement, since exercise is risky at his age
ask.why: An intense start could be unsafe with a heart condition, and avoiding all movement may miss real benefits. Asking his doctor first keeps him safe, and a gentle activity that involves learning, like simple yoga or dance steps, may exercise his mind as well as his body.

chapters.take: Learning new moves may train the brain as well as the body, at any age.

story.b: Eight weeks later, Kavya walks into the last mock test before the entrance exam. She is nervous, but it is a familiar, manageable kind of nervous. Her days still revolve around study. But they now include ten minutes of skipping before evening sessions, a brisk walk after dinner, the stairs during afternoon breaks and badminton with Ruchi on Sundays. Her back aches less, and the afternoon fog comes less often. Her mock scores have crept up, though she knows many things helped. Ruchi still sees the counsellor and smiles more these days. On the family call that night, Nani shows off a new pose. Kavya no longer thinks of moving as time stolen from studying. It has become part of studying.

chapters.take: Moving your body regularly can help your mind feel sharper, calmer and happier.
